summary: Updates the Sieve reject extension from RFC 3028 so a message can be refused during delivery instead of by sending a bounce. This helps avoid contributing to floods of bounces after forged-sender spam. This is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3028 and updates RFC 5228.

eli5.summary: If a stranger sends junk and puts your name on it, sending a note back to you just adds to your mess. This lets the mail system say no right at the door.

questions: how to reject mail without sending bounce messages
difference between sieve reject and ereject
how to reject mail without sending a bounce
subtitle: Lets a Sieve mail filter refuse a message during delivery, so no bounce goes to a forged sender.

tldr.problem: The original Sieve reject action sent a Message Disposition Notification (MDN) to the envelope sender. When the sender address is forged, as in a Joe-job spam run, that notice lands on an innocent third party.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5429 lets reject refuse the message during the SMTP transaction when possible, and adds an ereject action that always prefers protocol-level refusal and only sends a report if the sender is not judged forged.
tldr.outcome: ereject is meant to replace reject wherever possible, especially for spam and virus rejections. RFC 5429 obsoletes RFC 3028 and updates RFC 5228.

today: RFC 5429 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3028 and updates RFC 5228. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Joe-Job Problem
sections.content:
A Joe-job is a spam run forged to look like it came from an innocent party, who is then flooded with automated bounces, MDNs and personal complaints. The original Sieve reject action in RFC 3028 required an MDN to be sent to the envelope sender, so it added to that flood.

The Sieve language in RFC 5228 does not define any reject action, which is why this document exists. It updates reject and defines a new ereject action. By refusing at the protocol level, an MDN is less likely to be needed and so less likely to be misdirected.

Implementations are also encouraged to use spam detection to judge the risk of sending an MDN, and may silently drop the MDN if the rejected message is likely spam.
sections.eli5: If someone pretends to be you when mailing junk, every 'sorry, no' reply goes to you. The fix is to refuse the junk before the mail is even accepted.

sections.title: The ereject Action
sections.content:
The syntax is ereject <reason: string>, and a script must declare the ereject capability. The action cancels the implicit keep and refuses delivery. The reason is a UTF-8 string. The Sieve interpreter MUST do the most preferred of two things that works, falling back if needed.

  • Refuse delivery with a 5XX response over SMTP or LMTP, which SHOULD be 550.
  • Send a non-delivery report (DSN) to the envelope sender, unless that address is judged forged or invalid.

Judging a sender forged is left to site-specific heuristics such as return-path verification. Implementations SHOULD log when a report is not sent and why. ereject MUST NOT be offered where protocol-level rejection is impossible, such as in a mail user agent.

SMTP does not allow non-US-ASCII reply text. If the reason contains it and no SMTP extension for UTF-8 replies is in use, the engine MUST replace the reason with an implementation-defined US-ASCII string. Anyone who wants the exact text kept should use reject.
sections.eli5: ereject says 'stop, not accepted' at the front door. Only if that is impossible does it send a written note, and never to an address that looks fake.

sections.title: The reject Action and Its Updates
sections.content:
The syntax is reject <reason: string>, with the reject capability. Unlike ereject, it always favors keeping the exact text of the reason, and typically refuses by sending a failure MDN back to the sender. That MDN must have the disposition deleted with the MDN-sent-automatically and automatic-action modes set. No MDN may be generated if the MAIL FROM or Return-Path is empty.

New in this RFC, an implementation MAY refuse over SMTP or LMTP instead, but only if the reason is US-ASCII (or a UTF-8 reply extension is negotiated), and either LMTP is used, or SMTP is used with a single recipient, or with several recipients who all refused delivery.

When an SMTP message has several accepted recipients and only some refuse, the server MUST accept the message and generate DSNs for the refusers, with an action-value of failed. LMTP can reject per recipient, so it does not need this.
sections.eli5: reject is the older, wordier way to say no. It keeps your exact message but usually mails it back, unless the mail system can say no at the door safely.

sections.title: Combining Actions and Upgrading Scripts
sections.content:
Both actions follow the same compatibility rules. Implementations MUST prohibit more than one reject in a script, and reject MUST be incompatible with vacation. It is NOT RECOMMENDED to combine reject with actions that deliver mail, like keep, fileinto and redirect, because it breaks the principle that a message is either delivered or bounced. The RFC admits that some organizations are legally required to archive everything, and that saving copies for analysis can be useful.

Implementations MUST NOT silently upgrade reject to ereject in a script, as this might change behavior the owner does not expect. Script generators SHOULD use ereject for anti-spam and anti-virus rejections and MAY upgrade older scripts, provided the target environment supports it.
sections.eli5: You can either say 'no, go away' or 'yes, come in', not both. And nobody should swap your polite no for a firm one behind your back.

sections.title: Protocol-Level Refusal in Practice
sections.content:
If the reason has several CRLF-separated lines, it MUST be returned as a multiline SMTP or LMTP response, and no line may exceed the SMTP line limit. A server that supports RFC 2034 enhanced codes MUST prepend one, with 5.7.1 or the more generic 5.7.0 RECOMMENDED.

The RFC's example script refuses a message when spamtest scores at least 6, and files it into a folder called Suspect at 4 or more. In SMTP the refusal appears after the DATA command as a multiline 550- reply.

An implementation that does not want to reveal why it rejected, for example that it detected spam, may first answer with a 4XX code on the first delivery attempt and send the 550 later.
sections.eli5: Saying no at the door is a short back-and-forth: the sender hands over the mail, and the receiver answers right away, 'no, and here is why'.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
The RFC says rejecting before delivery is better than accepting and bouncing. It warns that the explicit permission to silently drop a non-delivery report may enable denial-of-service situations, because techniques like spam checking and return-path verification have false positives. Care must be taken not to lose legitimate messages by failing to tell the sender they were not delivered.

For auto-responder issues it points to RFC 3834, and says ereject raises no security considerations beyond those of base Sieve. IANA is asked to update the reject registration and to replace the preliminary registration of the Sieve refuse extension with ereject.
sections.eli5: The risk is staying quiet when you should not: if your fake-sender check is wrong, a real person never learns their mail was refused.
